name: C++
title: Modern C++ from the first line
intro: C++ began in the 1980s as C with classes and grew into one of the most widely used languages for programs that must be fast: games and game engines, browsers, databases, trading systems, embedded devices and much of the software other programs run on. Modern C++ (C++11 and later) is a different experience from the old style: the standard library manages memory and collections for you, and you rarely write new or delete. These lessons use C++20. Every example is a whole program and shows exactly what it prints. To run one yourself, save it as hello.cpp and type g++ -std=c++20 -o hello hello.cpp && ./hello.

sections.p: A C++ program starts in main. #include <iostream> brings in the input/output library, and std::cout << ... sends values to the screen, one << after another. Nothing ends the line unless you print '\n'. std:: says the name comes from the standard library.
std::string is a real text type that grows as needed. + joins strings, size() gives the length, and you can compare them with ==.

practice.why: Each << adds the next piece right after the last one. The spaces are inside the strings.
2 + 3 outside quotes is arithmetic. Inside quotes it is just text.

practice.q: Why do lessons write std::cout and not just cout?
options: cout lives in the std namespace
It is a different, faster cout
It is required on Windows only
practice.answer: cout lives in the std namespace
practice.why: The standard library puts its names in namespace std so they don't clash with yours.

lessons.title: Types, auto and const
lessons.summary: int, double, bool, integer division, auto and const.

sections.p: Every variable has a type that is fixed when it is declared. Dividing two ints drops the fraction; if either side is a double, you get a fractional answer. auto lets the compiler work the type out from the value. bool prints as 1 or 0 unless you ask for std::boolalpha.

const means a value cannot change after it is set; the compiler refuses any attempt. Make things const by default and you get fewer surprises. constexpr goes further and computes the value while compiling.

practice.why: 9 / 2 divides two ints and drops the fraction. With 9.0 the arithmetic is done in double.
Without std::boolalpha, a bool prints as 1 for true and 0 for false.

practice.q: What type does auto x = 2.5; give x?
practice.why: A literal with a decimal point is a double, so x is a double.

lessons.title: Functions and references
lessons.summary: Passing by value, by reference and by const reference.

sections.p: Arguments are copied by default, so a function cannot change the caller's variable. A reference parameter, written int&, is another name for the caller's variable, so changes stick. For big values you only read, use const T&: no copy, and no changes allowed.
Several functions can share a name if their parameter types differ. The compiler picks the one that matches the arguments.

practice.why: x is a reference to n, so each call doubles n itself: 3, 6, 12.
x is a copy, so setting it to 0 doesn't touch n.

practice.q: Why pass a std::string as const std::string&?
options: To avoid copying it while promising not to change it
So the function can change it
practice.answer: To avoid copying it while promising not to change it
practice.why: A reference avoids the copy, and const keeps the caller's string safe.

lessons.title: Vectors, maps and algorithms
lessons.summary: std::vector, range-for, std::map and the <algorithm> header.

sections.p: std::vector<int> is a growable array: push_back adds to the end, size() counts, and v[i] reads by index from 0. A range-for loop, for (int n : v), visits every element. <algorithm> and <numeric> have ready-made loops such as std::sort and std::accumulate.

std::map<K, V> stores keys with values, sorted by key. m[key] reads or creates an entry (a new int starts at 0), and contains (C++20) checks without creating one. A range-for over a map gives key-value pairs, which structured bindings can unpack.

practice.why: Adding 7 makes four elements, and index 1 is the second one, 5.
std::map keeps its keys sorted, whatever order they were added in.
int x is a copy of each element. Write int& x to change the vector itself.

lessons.title: Classes and RAII
lessons.summary: Members, constructors, destructors, and virtual functions.

sections.p: A class bundles data with the functions that work on it, and private members can only be touched by those functions. A constructor sets an object up; the destructor (~Name) runs automatically when the object goes out of scope. Tying cleanup to the destructor is called RAII, and it is how C++ manages files, locks and memory without forgetting to release them.
A class can inherit from another. Mark a function virtual in the base class and override in the derived one, and calls through a base reference reach the derived version.

practice.why: n is destroyed at the closing brace of its block, before end is printed.
id is virtual, so the call through a Base reference reaches Child's version.

practice.q: What does RAII mean in practice?
options: Cleanup happens in destructors, automatically at the end of scope
Objects can only be created with new
practice.answer: Cleanup happens in destructors, automatically at the end of scope
practice.why: Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation: an object owns its resource and its destructor releases it.

sections.p: A template is code with a type left open: the compiler writes a version for each type you use. The standard containers are templates, which is why you write std::vector<int>.

When you do need an object on the heap, hold it in a std::unique_ptr: it deletes the object when it goes out of scope, so you never call delete yourself. A lambda, [capture](params) { body }, is a small unnamed function, often passed to algorithms; the capture list says which outside variables it may use.

practice.why: The template makes an int version and a double version. 1.5 + 1.5 is 3, which prints as 3.
[base] captures a copy of base when the lambda is made, so changing base afterwards has no effect. [&base] would capture by reference.

practice.q: Why prefer std::unique_ptr over new and delete?
options: It deletes the object automatically, so nothing leaks
It allows many owners at once
It stores the object on the stack
practice.answer: It deletes the object automatically, so nothing leaks
practice.why: unique_ptr owns the object and frees it in its destructor. std::shared_ptr is the one for shared ownership.

sections.p: std::string owns its characters and grows as needed, so the C worries about sizes and zero bytes go away. It knows its size(), joins with +, compares with ==, and has members such as find (which returns std::string::npos when nothing is found) and substr.
sections.out:
hazelnut has 8 letters
true
nut starts at 5: hazel
no oak

sections.p: A std::string_view is a cheap window onto characters that live somewhere else: a pointer and a length, nothing copied. It is the usual parameter type for a function that only reads text, because a std::string, a literal or part of either can be passed without making a copy. The one rule is that the characters must outlive the view.

C++20's std::format builds a string from a pattern, like Python's f-strings. Each {} is replaced by the next argument; inside the braces :>6 right-aligns in 6 columns, :<8 left-aligns, and :.2f gives two decimals. Unlike printf, it checks the types when it compiles.
sections.out:
Sam found 42 nuts
[oak     ] [    17]
0.10 kg each
echo and echo again

practice.why: Adding "s" makes 6 letters. substr(1, 3) takes 3 characters starting at index 1.
> pads on the left so the value sits on the right; < does the opposite.

practice.q: Why is std::string_view a good parameter type for a function that only reads text?
options: Strings and literals can be passed without copying
It can change the caller's string
It adds a zero byte at the end
It is the only type std::format accepts
practice.answer: Strings and literals can be passed without copying
practice.why: A view is just a pointer and a length to characters stored elsewhere.

lessons.title: Errors: exceptions and std::optional
lessons.summary: Reporting failure, and cleaning up when it happens.

sections.p: When a function cannot do its job, it can throw an exception. The function stops at once, and so does every caller, until a try block with a matching catch is found. The standard library's exceptions derive from std::exception, and what() returns the message. std::stoi, which turns text into an int, throws std::invalid_argument when the text is not a number.
sections.out:
left: 6
error: only 6 nuts left
not a number

sections.p: When an exception passes through a function, every local object in it is destroyed, so its destructor runs. This is why RAII (from the classes lesson) matters: a file, a lock or memory owned by an object is released however the function ends, with no finally needed.
sections.out:
open store
close store
caught: squirrel startled

sections.h: std::optional for answers that may be missing
sections.p: Not finding something is often normal, not exceptional. std::optional<T> holds either a T or nothing (std::nullopt). Test it like a bool, read it with *, or use value_or to supply a default.

practice.why: throw jumps straight to the catch, skipping "c"; the program then carries on after the try block.
a holds 5; b is empty, so value_or gives 10.

practice.q: Why don't C++ programs need a finally block to release resources?
options: Destructors of local objects run when an exception passes through
The operating system frees everything immediately
practice.answer: Destructors of local objects run when an exception passes through
practice.why: With RAII, owning a resource in an object guarantees it is released however the scope ends.

lessons.title: Value types and operators
lessons.summary: Making your own types behave like built-in ones.

sections.p: You can define what +, == or << mean for your own types. A small type that holds a value, such as an amount of money or a point, then reads as naturally as an int. Overload operators only where the meaning is obvious; a + that does something surprising makes code harder to read.

C++20 can write comparisons for you. Declaring operator== and operator<=> (the "spaceship") as = default compares the members in order, and from those the compiler provides !=, <, >, <= and >=. Sorting a vector of such values then needs no extra code.

practice.why: The operator multiplies each member by k.

practice.q: What does = default on operator<=> do?
options: Compares the members one by one, in the order they are declared
practice.answer: Compares the members one by one, in the order they are declared
practice.why: The first member that differs decides; that is why 1.2 comes before 1.10 here.

practice.q: Why does operator<< return the std::ostream&?
options: So that calls can be chained: cout << a << b
practice.answer: So that calls can be chained: cout << a << b
practice.why: cout << a returns cout, and the next << is applied to it.

lessons.title: Lambdas and algorithms
lessons.summary: Small functions written in place, and the algorithms that use them.

sections.p: A lambda is a function written where it is used: [](int n) { return n * 2; }. The square brackets list what it captures from around it: [limit] copies limit in, [&total] uses total by reference so the lambda can change it. Lambdas are how you tell standard algorithms what to do.

C++20 ranges let algorithms take a whole container instead of a begin/end pair: std::ranges::sort(v). Views describe a lazy pipeline joined with |: filter keeps some elements and transform changes each one. Nothing is copied; the work happens as you loop over the result.

practice.why: [&count] captures by reference, so the lambda changes the real count.
[x] copies x when the lambda is created, while it is still 1.

options: Gives a lazy view of only the elements that pass a test
Copies matching elements into a new vector
practice.answer: Gives a lazy view of only the elements that pass a test
practice.why: Views don't change or copy the container; they decide what you see as you iterate.

lessons.title: Project: counting words
lessons.summary: Strings, maps, lambdas and formatting in one program.

sections.p: This program counts how often each word appears in a short text, ignoring case and punctuation, and prints the most common ones in a table. It reads words with a std::istringstream, cleans each one, counts with a std::map, copies the pairs into a vector, sorts them with a lambda (most frequent first, then alphabetically), and prints with std::format.
sections.out:
21 words, 12 different
the       5
nut       3
a         2
squirrel  2

sections.p: Skip short words such as "a" and "the" with a set of stop words, or read the text from a file with std::ifstream. If you need the order of first appearance rather than alphabetical ties, record the position where each word was first seen.

practice.q: Why copy the map's pairs into a vector before sorting?
options: A std::map always keeps its keys in order, so it cannot be re-sorted by count
practice.answer: A std::map always keeps its keys in order, so it cannot be re-sorted by count
practice.why: The map's order is fixed by its keys; a vector can be put in any order.
m["nut"] creates the entry with 0 the first time, then ++ counts; there are two different keys.

practice.q: What does in >> word do with an std::istringstream?
options: Reads the next word, skipping spaces
Reads the rest of the text
practice.answer: Reads the next word, skipping spaces
practice.why: >> into a std::string stops at whitespace, and the loop ends when no words are left.
